doc_summary: Buck Shlegeris analyzes, under a conservative adversarial assumption, how scheming models could collude when used as untrusted monitors, centering on whether the monitor can tell synthetic attacks from real ones, and proposes anti-collusion mechanisms. A large part concerns what makes synthetic inputs detectable as fake and how to make them harder to distinguish.

items.claim: In a setup, build synthetic test cases by taking real contexts and minimally modifying them to contain the target behaviour, refreshed regularly, instead of generating wholly synthetic scenarios upfront, because wholly fabricated contexts carry tells.
items.quote: Instead of just producing synthetic attacks upfront, you can construct synthetic attacks by taking real contexts and modifying them minimally to contain attacks, and rerun this process regularly throughout deployment.

items.claim: Prefers assuming models can detect fakes by default over trusting that synthetic inputs look real, because models are trained on huge text quantities and know patterns humans cannot anticipate, making it hard to be sure none of the faked material has tells.
items.quote: it might be a huge amount of effort, and it might be really hard to be sure that none of the stuff you faked has any tells (especially given that models have been trained on huge quantities of text and know about many patterns that we don't).

items.claim: In a setup, ensure transcript text attributed to the target model is something it would plausibly have generated itself instead of inserting prefilled or scripted words, because models notice when words have been 'put in their mouth' and respond by becoming more cautious.
items.quote: models might naturally be able to notice when words have been “put in their mouth”--that is, when a context contains text that they supposedly generated, but that they actually would be very unlikely to generate.

items.claim: Expect models to behave more conservatively when they recognise an input as an intentionally tricky synthetic test, so apparent good behaviour on eval-like inputs is weak evidence about real-deployment behaviour.
items.quote: Models might find it very salient when they're being run on synthetic inputs, because there's strong incentive to behave more conservatively when you're being run on an intentionally tricky synthetic input

items.claim: In a setup, reduce or paraphrase the context the model sees (redact prior tool outputs, rewrite surface text) instead of supplying long full-fidelity fabricated histories, because less context leaves fewer tells that reveal the input is fake.
items.quote: If you can reduce the amount of context the monitor sees, it's less likely to notice tells that allow it to realize that the input was fake.

items.claim: Validate realism of synthetic material empirically by testing whether a model can be trained to tell synthetic from genuine on-policy examples; if it cannot, the synthetic attacks are likelier to pass as real.
items.quote: construct a dataset of innocuous off-policy actions (e.g. ask one of the people who is in charge of generating synthetic attacks to generate some synthetic innocuous actions that they think look like actions the policy would take in the course of a normal trajectory)

items.claim: In a setup, avoid fixed environment features that differ from what the model expects at deployment time, because a deployment context that evolves in ways salient to the model and hard to fake can mark test scenarios as fake.
items.quote: it's pretty reasonable to expect that the deployment environment of the AI agent will change substantially after it has been deployed for a while, in a way that is easy and salient for the model to notice and hard for us to fake.

items.claim: Prefers adversarial analysis that models the AI as a strategic opponent over assuming benign or naive behaviour, because conservative assumptions protect against the worst case; defences are developed by iterating red-team and blue-team moves to equilibrium.
items.quote: we just tried different collusion strategies and then investigated various defenses that we thought might break them, and then iterated on both sides until we reached an equilibrium.

items.claim: Distrusts inferring scheming from evaluation performance alone, because the evidence is too noisy to support confident updates about a model's capability or intent.
items.quote: we probably won't be confident about e.g. whether the model is capable enough notice a certain class of attacks 99% of the time or 99.9% of the time, and so probably can't make that much of an update based on evaluation.

items.claim: Prefers testing the monitor over honeypotting the policy with synthetic inputs, because a policy can attack at a rate around 1/N and evade synthetic-input search, while the monitor cannot adopt a rare-failure strategy.
items.quote: the policy has a conceptually easy strategy to counter synthetic input tests: it can choose a low probability of attacking on any particular input, such that it's very hard for you to find an input where it attacks

items.claim: Open problem: research whether models can detect off-policy actions under countermeasures, and how to evaluate models' ability to play Schelling games.
items.quote: (I'd love to see research on whether models are able to detect off-policy actions given various countermeasures.)
